course.title: Timeline Analysis
course.description: A practical, research-driven course in digital forensic timeline analysis. It teaches time semantics, filesystem and operating-system timestamps, application and network artifacts, Plaso and Sleuth Kit workflows, Autopsy and Timesketch analysis, temporal correlation, clock-skew reasoning, filtering, performance, anomaly investigation, provenance, reproducibility, and defensible reporting. The final project integrates these skills into an auditable Python timeline-analysis workbench.
prerequisites: Basic Python programming with CSV, functions, and exceptions
Foundational digital-forensics concepts such as evidence preservation and hashing
An authorized forensic lab or legally obtained training dataset
learningOutcomes: Explain timeline analysis and super timelines while separating evidence observations from interpretations.
Normalize offset-aware timestamps to UTC while preserving original representations.
Construct and interpret filesystem timelines using Sleuth Kit body files and mactime.
Interpret Windows FILETIME and Windows Event Log evidence in context.
Use Plaso log2timeline, pinfo, psort, and psteal workflows.
Design targeted collection and event filters while documenting their blind spots.
Correlate filesystem, OS, application, registry, browser, and network observations.
Estimate candidate clock skew from multiple reference events.
Use Autopsy and Timesketch concepts to navigate large timelines.
Investigate missing data, duplicates, anomalies, and parser limitations.
Create reproducibility records with commands, filters, hashes, and time assumptions.
Write source-linked findings that state uncertainty and limitations.
Build and explain an auditable Python timeline-analysis workbench.

modules.title: Foundations of Timeline Analysis
modules.description: Time semantics, evidence workflow, provenance, and forensic reasoning.

lessons.title: Scope and Purpose of Timeline Analysis
lessons.description: Learn what a forensic timeline is, what questions it can answer, and why a timeline is a derived analytical view rather than a replacement for source evidence.
learningObjectives: explain timeline analysis in forensic terms
identify questions that timelines answer well

notes.text: Timeline analysis as evidence correlation

Timeline analysis orders timestamped observations from one or more evidence sources so an analyst can reconstruct sequence, identify activity windows, and compare independent records. A super timeline aggregates many source types into one chronological dataset.

items: A timeline event is an observation tied to a source; an inference is an analyst conclusion based on one or more observations.
Useful questions include what occurred before or after a known event, which sources corroborate a window, and where activity is unusually dense.
A single timestamp rarely establishes who performed an action or why it happened.
Preserve source, parser, path/record identifier, and original timestamp information for important events.

notes.text: Never describe temporal proximity alone as proof of causality or user intent.

quiz.question: What is a timeline event most safely treated as?
options: A timestamped observation from an evidence source
quiz.answer: A timestamped observation from an evidence source
quiz.explanation: The event must be interpreted using source semantics and corroborating evidence.

summary: Timelines are derived chronological views of timestamped observations.
Strong conclusions require provenance and corroboration.

lessons.title: UTC, Offsets, and Time Zones
lessons.description: Build the time-normalization skills required to compare timestamps produced by systems in different zones.
learningObjectives: explain why local time without an offset is ambiguous

notes.text: RFC 3339 defines a profile of ISO 8601 for Internet timestamps. A numeric offset such as +05:30 identifies the relationship between local time and UTC. A trailing Z denotes UTC.

from datetime import datetime, timezone
raw = "2026-01-15T10:30:00+05:30"
dt = datetime.fromisoformat(raw)
print(dt.astimezone(timezone.utc).isoformat())

items: Preserve the original representation and create a separate normalized field.
Daylight-saving transitions change local offsets and can create confusing local displays.
Do not infer a timezone from a filename, IP address, or analyst expectation when the evidence can provide a more direct basis.
For forensic correlation, UTC is a useful common representation, but original source semantics must remain available.

quiz.question: What does +05:30 indicate?
quiz.answer: 5:30 ahead of UTC
quiz.explanation: The numeric offset states the local clock is five hours and thirty minutes ahead of UTC.

summary: Use explicit offsets when normalizing time.
Keep original timestamps alongside normalized values.

lessons.title: Clock Skew and Synchronization
lessons.description: Understand clock skew, NTP, drift, and why a timeline may contain inconsistent clock readings.
learningObjectives: identify evidence needed before applying a clock correction

notes.text: Clock skew is the difference between a system clock and a reference or another system. NTP is widely used to synchronize clocks, but an analyst should not assume synchronization simply because NTP is configured.

items: Use multiple independent reference events when estimating skew.
Clock drift can make a single offset invalid over a long interval.
A manual clock change can create a discontinuity rather than a stable offset.
Preserve original timestamps and store any adjusted time as a derived value.

notes.text: Do not globally shift a timeline from one timestamp pair without testing additional anchors.

quiz.question: Why use multiple reference events for skew estimation?
options: To test whether an offset is stable
quiz.answer: To test whether an offset is stable
quiz.explanation: Multiple anchors help distinguish stable skew from bad references or clock changes.

summary: Clock correction is an inference that needs evidence.
NTP configuration is not by itself proof of correct historical time.

lessons.title: Forensic Workflow, Integrity, and Provenance
lessons.description: Place timeline analysis inside a defensible evidence workflow from scope through reporting.
learningObjectives: explain the role of evidence integrity

items: Define the investigative question and scope.
Preserve or acquire evidence according to authorized procedures.
Record evidence identifiers and integrity values.
Parse evidence into derived timeline data.
Normalize and correlate events without discarding provenance.
Validate key findings against independent sources.
Report observations, interpretations, and limitations.

notes.text: NIST SP 800-86 provides practical guidance for integrating forensic techniques into incident response and emphasizes the need to consider organizational and legal requirements.

items: Record tool names, versions, command lines, filters, time assumptions, and output hashes.
Keep derived timelines distinguishable from source evidence.
A file hash checks byte-level integrity of that file; it does not prove semantic correctness or completeness.

quiz.question: What does provenance primarily enable?
options: Tracing a derived event back to its source and processing steps
quiz.answer: Tracing a derived event back to its source and processing steps
quiz.explanation: Provenance supports review and reproducibility.

summary: Timeline work is part of a broader forensic workflow.
Integrity and provenance make derived analysis reviewable.

modules.title: Filesystem and Operating-System Timelines
modules.description: Filesystem activity, Sleuth Kit timelines, Windows FILETIME, and Event Log evidence.

lessons.title: Filesystem Timeline Concepts
lessons.description: Interpret filesystem metadata timelines and understand their limits.
learningObjectives: distinguish metadata evidence from user attribution

notes.text: Filesystem timelines represent temporal metadata associated with files and filesystem structures. The Sleuth Kit documents a workflow in which temporal data is gathered and then sorted into a timeline.

items: Modification, metadata/status change, access, and creation/birth timestamps have different semantics and availability.
Filesystem timestamps can be changed by normal system operations, copying, restoration, software behavior, and filesystem-specific rules.
MACB is a compact activity representation; analysts should inspect the underlying timestamps when precision matters.

notes.text: A file modification timestamp does not prove that a person manually edited the file.

quiz.question: What does a filesystem timestamp most directly describe?
quiz.answer: A filesystem-recorded temporal property
quiz.explanation: The timestamp is metadata whose semantics depend on the filesystem and artifact.

summary: Filesystem timelines are valuable but source-specific.
Interpret timestamps according to filesystem semantics.

lessons.title: Sleuth Kit Body Files and mactime
lessons.description: Construct a classic filesystem activity timeline using body-file data.
learningObjectives: trace timeline rows back to filesystem metadata

notes.text: The Sleuth Kit body file is a pipe-delimited intermediate representation. Its documented TSK 3.x form includes fields such as name, inode, size, atime, mtime, ctime, and crtime. mactime reads body-file data and sorts it into a timeline.

fls -m C:/ -r image.dd > body.txt
mactime -b body.txt > timeline.txt

items: The exact partition offset and filesystem type must be determined from the evidence, not copied blindly.
The body file is derived data; preserve the source image and record the collection command.
Time-skew adjustment options exist, but adjustments must be documented and justified.

practicals.title: Build a basic TSK timeline
practicals.description: Generate a body file from a permitted lab image and convert it to a sorted activity timeline.
steps: Work from an authorized forensic image or copy.
Determine the relevant filesystem and partition offset.
Run fls recursively with a mount point label.
Run mactime against the resulting body file.
Inspect several entries and record their source paths.
practicals.solution:
fls -m C:/ -r -o <partition_offset> lab-image.dd > body.txt
mactime -b body.txt > timeline.txt
practicals.output: The result is a chronologically ordered text timeline derived from filesystem metadata. Exact entries depend on the image.

quiz.question: What does mactime do in the classic TSK workflow?
options: Sort body-file temporal data into a timeline
quiz.answer: Sort body-file temporal data into a timeline
quiz.explanation: TSK describes timeline creation as data gathering followed by sorting/merging with mactime.

summary: Body files provide an intermediate temporal representation.
mactime sorts and presents that representation.

lessons.title: Windows FILETIME and NTFS Semantics
lessons.description: Decode Windows FILETIME and understand the difference between stored UTC values and displayed local time.
learningObjectives: explain the FILETIME epoch and unit

notes.text: Microsoft documents FILETIME as a 64-bit value containing 100-nanosecond intervals since 1601-01-01 UTC. Microsoft also documents different timestamp behavior across filesystems; NTFS stores file times in UTC, while FAT uses local-time semantics.

from datetime import datetime, timezone, timedelta
FILETIME_EPOCH = datetime(1601, 1, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
value = 133801248000000000
seconds = value / 10_000_000
print((FILETIME_EPOCH + timedelta(seconds=seconds)).isoformat())
High numeric precision does not imply high real-world accuracy. Timestamp update rules and filesystem semantics still matter.

practicals.title: Convert FILETIME to UTC
practicals.description: Convert a Windows FILETIME integer using only Python's standard library.
steps: Divide the FILETIME count by 10,000,000 to obtain seconds.
Add the duration to the epoch.
practicals.solution:
from datetime import datetime, timezone, timedelta
FILETIME_EPOCH = datetime(1601, 1, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
value = 133801248000000000
seconds = value / 10_000_000
print((FILETIME_EPOCH + timedelta(seconds=seconds)).isoformat())
practicals.output: A timezone-aware UTC datetime is produced; the exact value follows from the supplied integer.

quiz.question: What is the FILETIME epoch?
quiz.explanation: Microsoft defines FILETIME relative to January 1, 1601 UTC.

summary: FILETIME is a numeric representation, not a statement about user behavior.
Filesystem documentation is essential for interpreting timestamp semantics.

lessons.title: Windows Event Log as a Timeline Source
lessons.description: Use structured Windows event records as corroborating timeline evidence.
learningObjectives: filter events by time and metadata
explain why event IDs require context

notes.text: Windows Event Log provides structured records associated with event providers and channels. PowerShell Get-WinEvent supports filtering by log name, provider, event ID, time range, user ID, data, and XML queries.

Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-1); EndTime=Get-Date} |
  Select-Object TimeCreated,Id,ProviderName,Message

items: An event ID should be interpreted with its provider, channel, and event data.
Keep the original event log where required; rendered CSV is a derived view.
TimeCreated is one part of an event's meaning; message/data fields may contain the context needed for correlation.

practicals.title: Extract a bounded Windows event window
practicals.description: Export a small, reproducible set of Windows events from an authorized lab host.
steps: Use Get-WinEvent with FilterHashtable or FilterXml.
Select time, ID, provider, and relevant data.
practicals.solution: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-1); EndTime=Get-Date} | Select-Object TimeCreated,Id,ProviderName,Message | Export-Csv -NoTypeInformation system-window.csv
practicals.output: The CSV contains events matching the selected filter. Exact rows depend on the host and time window.

quiz.question: Why interpret an event ID with its provider?
options: The provider supplies the event source/schema context
quiz.answer: The provider supplies the event source/schema context
quiz.explanation: Windows Event Log associates event definitions with providers and schemas.

summary: Structured event logs add semantic context beyond a timestamp.
Bounded queries make extraction reproducible.

tasks.title: Correlate a File Change with an OS Event
tasks.description: Correlate a filesystem event with nearby Windows log records while separating temporal proximity from causality.
tasks.problemStatement: Given a permitted lab CSV containing file events and Windows events, identify plausible corroborating events within a stated window.
requirements: CSV exports from a lab dataset
tasks.hint: Normalize timestamps before comparing them; never compare local strings directly.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The script identifies records within five minutes of an evidence-backed anchor. The result is corroboration candidates, not a causal proof.

modules.title: Artifact-Centered Timeline Construction
modules.description: Application artifacts, Plaso extraction, parser coverage, and filtering.

lessons.title: Application and User-Activity Artifacts
lessons.description: Use browser, shell, document, and application artifacts as contextual timeline sources.
learningObjectives: correlate application artifacts with OS evidence

notes.text: Application artifacts can add semantic context that filesystem metadata lacks. Browser records may contain visit times and URLs; shell history may contain commands; document metadata may contain application-specific times; application logs can record domain-specific events.

items: Artifact retention varies by application and configuration.
A browser history record is not necessarily proof of a successful network transaction or direct user interaction.
Shell history may be incomplete, edited, disabled, or affected by shell behavior.
Use independent OS and application sources when the conclusion matters.

quiz.question: Why combine application and filesystem evidence?
options: They can provide different context and corroboration
quiz.answer: They can provide different context and corroboration
quiz.explanation: Different sources can constrain the interpretation of an event.

summary: Application artifacts add semantics but have source-specific limitations.
Corroborate important activity with independent sources.

lessons.title: Plaso Architecture and Workflow
lessons.description: Learn the practical Plaso pipeline for extracting, inspecting, filtering, and exporting timeline events.
learningObjectives: describe log2timeline, pinfo, psort, and psteal
explain why packaged releases are preferred for normal use

notes.text: Plaso is a Python-based engine for automated timeline creation. Its user documentation describes log2timeline for extracting events, pinfo for inspecting storage files, psort for post-processing and analysis, and psteal as a shortcut combining extraction and post-processing.

log2timeline.py --storage-file case.plaso evidence.E01
pinfo.py --sections sources case.plaso
psort.py -o dynamic -w timeline.csv case.plaso

items: The Plaso storage file contains extracted events and metadata about collection and sources.
Use a packaged release for routine use; development releases can change frequently.
The exact parsers selected depend on the source and Plaso configuration.

practicals.title: Generate and inspect a Plaso timeline
practicals.description: Create a Plaso storage file and inspect its sources before exporting a timeline.
steps: Run log2timeline with a storage-file output.
Export a dynamic timeline with psort.
practicals.solution:
log2timeline.py --storage-file case.plaso evidence.E01
pinfo.py --sections sources case.plaso
psort.py -o dynamic -w timeline.csv case.plaso
practicals.output: The output includes a Plaso storage file and a CSV timeline. Exact events depend on the evidence.

quiz.question: Which tool post-processes Plaso storage files?
quiz.answer: psort
quiz.explanation: Plaso documents psort as the post-processing tool.

summary: Plaso separates extraction from post-processing.
The workflow should be recorded for reproducibility.

lessons.title: Parser Coverage and Provenance
lessons.description: Assess parser/source coverage instead of treating a generated timeline as complete.
learningObjectives: explain why parser success is not completeness

notes.text: A parser extracts supported structures from a source. A successful parse does not establish that all relevant information was present, collected, or supported.

items: Inspect source, parser, and extraction-error information for high-value events.
Document unsupported artifacts or parser limitations that could change the conclusion.
Keep targeted collections explicitly labeled as targeted.
Trace important events from exported rows back to their source representation.

practicals.title: Audit parser coverage
practicals.description: Use pinfo and an exported timeline to create a source/parser inventory.
steps: Record their source and parser fields.
Identify at least two possible coverage gaps.
Document how the gaps affect the investigative question.
practicals.solution:
pinfo.py --sections sources case.plaso
psort.py -o dynamic --fields datetime,timestamp_desc,source,source_long,message,parser -w audited.csv case.plaso
practicals.output: The deliverable is a coverage note identifying source/parser provenance and limitations.

quiz.question: Does successful parsing prove completeness?
options: No; parser and source coverage have limits
quiz.answer: No; parser and source coverage have limits
quiz.explanation: Parsing support is not evidence that all relevant data exists or was collected.

summary: Parser coverage is part of analytical validity.
Document limitations that affect the conclusion.

lessons.title: Collection Filters and Event Filters
lessons.description: Reduce noise using Plaso's documented collection and event-filter mechanisms.
learningObjectives: distinguish collection filters from event filters

notes.text: Collection filters restrict which source files are collected and parsed. Event filters operate on extracted events for selective export, analysis, or tagging. Plaso documents both mechanisms separately.

# Example documented-style Plaso event filter
data_type is 'syslog:line' and message_body contains 'root'

items: Use collection filters when source scope is intentionally narrow.
Use event filters when the broader dataset is already available but analysis needs a subset.
Record filters verbatim.
Retain the broader derived dataset when practical so a reviewer can reproduce a different selection.

practicals.title: Create a targeted Plaso workflow
practicals.description: Build a targeted collection and then filter extracted events.
steps: Create a YAML path filter for the relevant lab source.
Apply an event filter with psort.
Export the filtered results while retaining the storage file.
practicals.solution:
log2timeline.py --file-filter windows.yaml --storage-file targeted.plaso evidence.raw
pinfo.py --sections sources targeted.plaso
psort.py -o dynamic -w selected.csv targeted.plaso "data_type is 'syslog:line'"
practicals.output: The selected CSV contains only events matching the event filter. The storage file preserves the collected context.

quiz.question: What is the main danger of over-filtering?
quiz.answer: Loss of contextual events
quiz.explanation: Filtering can remove observations needed to interpret or corroborate a finding.

summary: Filtering is an analytical choice and should be documented.
Keep broader derived data when feasible.

tasks.title: Design a Targeted Collection Plan
tasks.description: Translate a Windows interactive-use question into a documented Plaso collection plan.
tasks.problemStatement: Design a targeted collection for a two-hour investigation window and explain included sources, exclusions, and blind spots.
tasks.hint: Start from the question, not from a favorite tool.
tasks.solutionCode:
description: Windows event logs for targeted timeline collection
type: include
path_separator: '\\'
paths:
  - '%SystemRoot%\\System32\\winevt\\Logs\\.+[.]evtx'
tasks.solutionExplanation: The filter demonstrates source-level selection. A real case should add other artifacts based on the actual question and document every inclusion/exclusion.

modules.title: Correlation, Visualization, and Investigation Views
modules.description: Super timelines, deduplication, event density, and Timesketch.

lessons.title: Super Timelines and Normalized Schemas
lessons.description: Combine heterogeneous events while preserving source-specific context.
learningObjectives: preserve original timestamp and provenance fields

notes.text: A super timeline combines timestamped observations from many source types into a common chronology. Plaso is explicitly designed for this use, while Autopsy and Timesketch provide analytical views over timeline data.

items: Useful fields include normalized datetime, original timestamp, source, source type, event type, message, user, host, parser, and source identifier.
Normalization should make events sortable without erasing original representation.
Do not assume every parser provides the same fields.
Correlation should be question-driven, not simply 'everything within one minute'.

quiz.question: What should a normalized timeline preserve?
options: Normalized time plus provenance and event context
quiz.answer: Normalized time plus provenance and event context
quiz.explanation: Sorting requires normalized time, while interpretation requires context and provenance.

summary: Super timelines make cross-source comparison possible.
A common schema should not erase source-specific meaning.

lessons.title: Deduplication and Event Identity
lessons.description: Remove exact duplicates safely and understand why timestamp-only deduplication is unsafe.
learningObjectives: explain why same-time events can be distinct

notes.text: Multi-source timelines can contain repeated records due to multiple parsers, exports, or derived representations. Deduplication is a transformation that should be auditable.
Do not deduplicate on timestamp alone. Two independent events can legitimately share an instant.

practicals.title: Implement exact deduplication
practicals.description: Remove only exact duplicate records from a CSV and report counts by source.
steps: Build a key from timestamp, source, event type, source ID, and message.
Write a cleaned CSV and report.
practicals.solution:
import csv
from collections import Counter
seen=set(); kept=[]; duplicates=Counter()
with open("timeline.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        key=(row["timestamp"],row["source"],row.get("event_type",""),row.get("source_id",""),row.get("message",""))
        if key in seen: duplicates[row["source"]] += 1
        else: seen.add(key); kept.append(row)
with open("timeline_dedup.csv","w",newline="",encoding="utf-8") as f:
    if kept:
        w=csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=kept[0].keys()); w.writeheader(); w.writerows(kept)
print(dict(duplicates))
practicals.output: Only exact duplicate records are removed; distinct same-time events remain.

quiz.question: Why is timestamp-only deduplication unsafe?
options: Different events can share a timestamp
quiz.answer: Different events can share a timestamp
quiz.explanation: A multi-source timeline can contain multiple legitimate observations at the same instant.

summary: Deduplication should preserve event identity.
Heuristic merging requires stronger evidence than identical timestamps.

lessons.title: Visualization and Event Density
lessons.description: Use visual and statistical views to identify candidate activity windows without equating volume with maliciousness.
learningObjectives: choose a visualization for an investigative question
use density as a triage signal

notes.text: Autopsy provides timeline views that show both activity volume and detailed events, while clustering reduces overload. Timesketch provides search, filters, charts, views, annotations, and stories.

items: A spike can represent normal updates, backups, indexing, or workload.
Use density to select windows for deeper source-level inspection.
The report should cite concrete events rather than merely a chart pattern.
Exploratory views are derived analytical aids, not replacements for source evidence.

practicals.title: Create an hourly density report
practicals.description: Count normalized events by UTC hour and identify candidate review windows.
steps: Select candidate windows using a transparent top-N or threshold rule.
practicals.solution:
from collections import Counter
from datetime import datetime, timezone
import csv
counts=Counter()
with open("timeline.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        dt=datetime.fromisoformat(row["timestamp"].replace("Z","+00:00")).astimezone(timezone.utc)
        counts[dt.replace(minute=0,second=0,microsecond=0)] += 1
for hour,count in sorted(counts.items()):
    print(hour.isoformat(), count)
practicals.output: The output highlights dense periods for manual investigation; it does not establish maliciousness.

quiz.question: What does an activity spike prove?
options: Nothing by itself; it identifies a review window
quiz.answer: Nothing by itself; it identifies a review window
quiz.explanation: Volume alone does not explain the cause of activity.

summary: Visualization helps navigate large timelines.
Density is a triage signal, not a conclusion.

lessons.title: Timesketch Case Organization
lessons.description: Use Timesketch sketches, timelines, searches, views, tags, and stories to organize collaborative analysis.
learningObjectives: describe how timelines are imported and explored
separate analyst annotations from source evidence

notes.text: Timesketch is an open-source collaborative forensic timeline analysis tool. Its documentation describes sketches as case-oriented containers that can include multiple timelines and views. Explore supports searches, time ranges, filters, saved views, and event annotations.

items: Tags, comments, stars, and stories are derived analyst context.
Timesketch documentation describes importing Plaso, CSV, and JSONL timelines.
Collaborative deployments require access control and secure handling because forensic timelines can contain sensitive evidence.

practicals.title: Create a Timesketch analysis workspace
practicals.description: Import a permitted timeline and create a reproducible investigative view.
steps: Deploy Timesketch using its documented lab method.
Create a sketch for the case.
Save a search/view and annotate a small set of events.
Record the search and filter parameters.
practicals.solution: Use the documented Timesketch web interface or API to create a sketch, import a supported timeline, apply a time range/filter, and save the resulting view.
practicals.output: The workspace contains a case sketch, imported timeline, reproducible view, and annotations. Exact UI labels can vary by release.

quiz.question: What is a Timesketch sketch used for?
options: Organizing case timelines and analysis context
quiz.answer: Organizing case timelines and analysis context
quiz.explanation: Timesketch documents sketches as case-oriented containers for timelines and analysis.

summary: Collaborative tools improve organization and reviewability.
Annotations are derived context, not original evidence.

tasks.title: Build an Auditable Timeline Normalizer
tasks.description: Create a Python utility that converts offset-aware timestamps to UTC while retaining the original values.
tasks.problemStatement: Given heterogeneous RFC 3339 timestamps, produce a normalized CSV and reject ambiguous timestamps.
tasks.hint: Use datetime.fromisoformat and astimezone(timezone.utc). Do not silently assume a timezone for naive input.
tasks.solutionCode:
import csv
from datetime import datetime, timezone

with open("input.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as src, open("normalized.csv","w",newline="",encoding="utf-8") as dst:
    r=csv.DictReader(src); fields=r.fieldnames+["normalized_utc"]; w=csv.DictWriter(dst,fieldnames=fields); w.writeheader()
    for row in r:
        raw=row["timestamp"]
        dt=datetime.fromisoformat(raw.replace("Z","+00:00"))
        if dt.tzinfo is None: raise ValueError("ambiguous timestamp: "+raw)
        row["normalized_utc"]=dt.astimezone(timezone.utc).isoformat().replace("+00:00","Z")
        w.writerow(row)
tasks.solutionExplanation: The utility refuses naive timestamps, preserving the analyst from silent timezone assumptions.

modules.title: Correlation, Skew, and Evidentiary Reasoning
modules.description: Temporal correlation, missing data, clock skew, and event sequencing.

lessons.title: Temporal Correlation and Context
lessons.description: Use time windows with host, user, process, and artifact context.

notes.text: Temporal correlation is most useful when the window is justified by the investigative question and expected event latency. A wider window is not automatically better.

items: Add host, user, process, path, network peer, or artifact identifiers where available.
Classify relationships as direct observation, temporal proximity, or corroborated inference.
Consider missing events and clock uncertainty before treating an ordering as meaningful.

quiz.question: What strengthens temporal correlation?
options: Choosing the window after seeing the answer
quiz.answer: Independent contextual evidence
quiz.explanation: Independent constraints reduce the chance of treating coincidence as causation.

summary: Temporal windows generate candidate relationships.
Context and source independence determine evidentiary strength.

lessons.title: Gaps, Missing Data, and Negative Evidence
lessons.description: Reason correctly about logging gaps, parser failures, retention, and absent records.
learningObjectives: distinguish absence of evidence from evidence of absence
identify common causes of timeline gaps
write bounded conclusions about missing data

notes.text: A timeline gap may reflect disabled logging, retention limits, parser failures, filtering, acquisition problems, clock errors, or simply the absence of an event. Silence in a dataset is not automatically proof that an action did not occur.

items: Check acquisition completeness and parser errors.
Check logging configuration and retention where available.
Look for independent sources covering the same interval.
Use language such as 'no supporting event was identified in the examined sources' when appropriate.

practicals.title: Write a missing-data assessment
practicals.description: Analyze an intentional logging gap and produce a defensible limitation statement.
steps: Check whether another source covers the interval.
Write a bounded conclusion and identify what additional evidence would help.
practicals.solution: A strong statement identifies the observable interval, missing source, plausible explanations, and remaining uncertainty.
practicals.output: The output is a limitation note, not a claim that the event definitely did or did not happen.

quiz.question: What does a known logging gap justify?
options: Proof the action did not happen
A statement that the source cannot support a conclusion for that interval
quiz.answer: A statement that the source cannot support a conclusion for that interval
quiz.explanation: The missing source creates uncertainty.

summary: Missingness is part of evidence interpretation.
Good analysts explicitly state observable boundaries.

lessons.title: Clock-Skew Estimation
lessons.description: Estimate candidate clock offsets from multiple reference events.

notes.text:
from datetime import datetime
pairs=[
("2026-01-15T10:00:00+00:00","2026-01-15T10:02:00+00:00"),
("2026-01-15T11:00:00+00:00","2026-01-15T11:01:50+00:00")]
for trusted, observed in pairs:
    print(datetime.fromisoformat(observed)-datetime.fromisoformat(trusted))
A single reference pair is insufficient to justify a global correction.

items: A stable offset should be supported by multiple reliable reference events.
Outliers may indicate weak anchors, drift, clock changes, or differing event semantics.
Keep any corrected timestamp as a derived field.

practicals.title: Estimate a candidate offset
practicals.description: Compare three paired timestamps and determine whether a stable skew is supported.
steps: Calculate observed minus trusted for each pair.
If justified, report an estimated offset and uncertainty.
practicals.solution:
from datetime import datetime
pairs=[('2026-01-15T10:00:00+00:00','2026-01-15T10:02:00+00:00'),('2026-01-15T11:00:00+00:00','2026-01-15T11:01:50+00:00'),('2026-01-15T12:00:00+00:00','2026-01-15T12:02:10+00:00')]
offsets=[datetime.fromisoformat(o)-datetime.fromisoformat(t) for t,o in pairs]
print([x.total_seconds() for x in offsets])
practicals.output: The output exposes the spread of candidate offsets. The analyst decides whether a stable correction is justified.

quiz.question: Why compare several offset estimates?
options: To test consistency and detect drift/outliers
quiz.answer: To test consistency and detect drift/outliers
quiz.explanation: Multiple anchors test whether the apparent skew is stable.

summary: Clock correction is an analytical inference.
Preserve original values after normalization or adjustment.

lessons.title: Event Sequencing and Causal Reasoning
lessons.description: Construct an evidence-backed sequence while distinguishing chronological order from causation.

items: Collect candidate events around the question window.
Normalize times while preserving originals.
Group by useful context such as host/user/process.
Order events with timestamp uncertainty in mind.
Identify independent corroboration.
Write observations first, then interpretations.
List credible alternatives when evidence is ambiguous.
Chronology is not causality.
Background processes can generate events unrelated to a preceding user action.
The strength of a sequence comes from source diversity and semantic context, not row count.

practicals.title: Produce an evidence-backed sequence
practicals.description: Turn a mixed event CSV into a concise six-step sequence.
steps: Select events that materially change the narrative.
Record source and event identifier for each.
Write an observation for each event.
Document one uncertainty or alternative explanation.
practicals.solution: The deliverable separates evidence observations from analytical interpretation.
practicals.output: The result is a reviewable chronology with source identifiers and explicit uncertainty.

quiz.question: What is the key distinction in a defensible sequence?
options: Observations are distinct from causal interpretations
quiz.answer: Observations are distinct from causal interpretations
quiz.explanation: A sequence can be chronological without proving causality.

summary: Good timeline analysis is disciplined evidence reasoning.
Report observations before conclusions.

tasks.title: Resolve a Cross-Host Time Discrepancy
tasks.description: Analyze overlapping events from two hosts and determine whether a stable clock offset is supported.
tasks.problemStatement: One host appears two minutes ahead, but one reference pair differs by five minutes. Evaluate the evidence and write a bounded conclusion.
tasks.hint: Do not discard the outlier without explaining why its semantics or reliability differ.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The code calculates each offset. The analyst must decide whether a correction is supported by multiple reliable anchors.

modules.title: Advanced Analysis, Performance, and Reporting
modules.description: Performance, query design, quality control, reproducibility, and reporting.

lessons.title: Performance and Triage
lessons.description: Scale analysis using bounded collection, filtering, search, and focused exports.

notes.text: Large timelines can contain millions of events. Targeted collection, event filtering, indexed search, and time-window triage reduce analysis cost. These are safe only when the reduction is documented and the broader dataset remains available when practical.

items: Start from the investigative question and time window.
Do not manually delete events without recording what was removed and why.
Use documented filters rather than undocumented spreadsheet editing for important findings.
Retain the unfiltered derived dataset where storage and policy permit.

quiz.question: What is a defensible performance optimization?
options: Use documented filters and preserve the broader dataset
quiz.answer: Use documented filters and preserve the broader dataset
quiz.explanation: Reproducible reduction lowers workload without silently destroying context.

summary: Performance should not come at the cost of traceability.
Document every reduction step.

lessons.title: Timeline Searching and Query Design
lessons.description: Write bounded searches using fields, time ranges, and Boolean conditions.
learningObjectives: test queries against expected matches and non-matches

notes.text: Plaso event filters support Boolean logic, comparisons, regular expressions, and date/time helpers. Timesketch provides search and filtering over its indexed timeline data.
data_type contains 'firefox' and message_body contains 'example.com'

items: Use actual fields exposed by the parser/dataset.
Test filters against known-positive and known-negative records.
A broad first search can be useful for discovery, followed by a narrower reproducible filter.

practicals.title: Design and test an event filter
practicals.description: Create a filter for a specific artifact family and content value.
steps: Choose a field documented for the dataset.
Test against known-positive and negative records.
Record the final expression and its purpose.
practicals.output: The filter should select events satisfying both conditions; exact matches depend on the dataset.

quiz.question: Why test both positive and negative examples?
options: To verify that the filter expresses the intended condition
quiz.answer: To verify that the filter expresses the intended condition
quiz.explanation: Testing catches silent over-selection and under-selection.

summary: Query design affects evidence selection.
Version and document important filters.

lessons.title: Quality Control and Reproducibility
lessons.description: Create a technical record that allows another analyst to reproduce a timeline result.
learningObjectives: trace a finding from source to timeline to report

items: Evidence identifier and integrity reference.
Tool and version information.
Source scope and paths.
Exact commands and filters.
Derived output hashes.
Timezone and normalization policy.
Known errors and limitations.
Important queries and conclusions.

notes.text:
sha256sum timeline.csv
sha256sum case.plaso
A hash verifies the bytes of the named file; it does not prove completeness or correct interpretation.

practicals.title: Create a reproducibility manifest
practicals.description: Write a JSON manifest for a timeline export.
practicals.output: The manifest records integrity and analytical context for the derived timeline.

quiz.question: What does a SHA-256 hash establish?
options: Byte-level integrity of the hashed file
quiz.answer: Byte-level integrity of the hashed file
quiz.explanation: The hash lets later users verify whether those file bytes changed.

summary: Reproducibility requires integrity plus provenance and procedure.
A hash is not a semantic correctness guarantee.

lessons.title: Reporting Defensible Findings
lessons.description: Write source-linked findings that distinguish observation, interpretation, confidence, and limitations.

notes.text: A strong timeline finding identifies the question, relevant window, observed records, source provenance, interpretation, and limitations. It avoids unsupported claims about intent, identity, or causality.

Observation: [timestamp] [source] recorded [event].
Correlation: [independent source] recorded [related event] within [window].
Interpretation: These observations are consistent with [bounded conclusion].
Limitations: [missing/uncertain evidence].

items: Observation answers what the source shows.
Interpretation explains what those observations may indicate.
Limitations identify uncertainty, gaps, parser coverage, and competing explanations.

practicals.title: Write one defensible finding
practicals.description: Select three related events and write a concise source-linked finding.
practicals.solution: A complete finding has Observation, Correlation, Interpretation, and Limitations sections.
practicals.output: The finding is reviewable because claims are tied to concrete event records.

quiz.question: Which statement is most defensible?
options: The user definitely attacked the system
The records are consistent with X, subject to stated limitations
quiz.answer: The records are consistent with X, subject to stated limitations
quiz.explanation: This language separates evidence from inference and communicates uncertainty.

summary: Reporting is part of technical analysis.
Every important conclusion should be traceable to evidence.

tasks.title: Create a Timeline QA Package
tasks.description: Validate a timeline CSV, report malformed timestamps, check ordering, and create a SHA-256 manifest.
tasks.problemStatement: Build a small Python QA utility for a normalized timeline.
tasks.hint: Report malformed rows rather than silently dropping them.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The QA package separates structural/data-quality errors from analytical findings and preserves a hash of the input.

modules.title: Advanced Artifact Correlation and Anomaly Analysis
modules.description: Registry, browser/network correlation, anomalies, and derived enrichment.

lessons.title: Registry Artifacts and System Context
lessons.description: Use registry-derived events as contextual evidence without overclaiming.
learningObjectives: distinguish user and system hive context
correlate registry observations with other sources

notes.text: Registry artifacts can provide information about users, configuration, applications, devices, and system state. Their usefulness depends on the specific key, hive, parser, and timestamp semantics.

items: A registry key last-write time is not direct proof of a human action.
User hives and system hives answer different questions.
Correlate registry observations with filesystem and event-log records.
Record hive/key paths and parser provenance for important events.

quiz.question: What does a registry key last-write time most safely establish?
options: A registry state-change timestamp subject to source semantics
quiz.answer: A registry state-change timestamp subject to source semantics
quiz.explanation: It is evidence of registry state change, not direct attribution.

summary: Registry artifacts provide system context.
Metadata timestamps should not be translated into unsupported human actions.

lessons.title: Browser and Network Correlation
lessons.description: Correlate browser records with DNS, proxy, firewall, and application evidence while respecting visibility limits.
learningObjectives: explain why a browser event may lack a matching network record

notes.text: Browser artifacts and network logs observe different layers. Browser history may reflect stored application state, while DNS/proxy/firewall logs depend on network architecture, caching, retention, and visibility.

items: Background requests and caching can produce activity without direct user interaction.
A browser URL may not generate a visible DNS event in the examined resolver logs.
Use host, user, process, URL, hostname, and source identifiers when available.
Absence in one network source is a visibility limitation, not proof of no traffic.

practicals.title: Correlate browser and DNS records
practicals.description: Build a correlation table from browser and DNS CSV files.
steps: Match hostname plus a justified time window.
Classify browser-only, DNS-only, and matched observations.
practicals.solution: Normalize timestamps, then correlate by hostname and time; keep unmatched records rather than discarding them.
practicals.output: The table distinguishes matched observations from one-source-only observations.

quiz.question: Why might a browser event have no DNS record?
options: Caching, resolver visibility, retention, or architecture
quiz.answer: Caching, resolver visibility, retention, or architecture
quiz.explanation: Network visibility depends on how the environment resolves and logs DNS.

summary: Browser and network evidence complement each other.
Interpret missing network records in the context of architecture and retention.

lessons.title: Timeline Anomalies and Anti-Forensics
lessons.description: Investigate inconsistent timestamps without treating anomalies as proof of manipulation.

notes.text: Anomalies can include impossible ordering, sudden clock jumps, inconsistent offsets, or conflicts between sources. They may result from clock changes, parser interpretation, copying, application behavior, or deliberate manipulation.

items: Compare independent time sources before asserting manipulation.
Preserve original timestamp representations.
Look for repeated patterns rather than one suspicious value.
State alternative benign explanations when evidence does not discriminate.

practicals.title: Investigate a timestamp anomaly
practicals.description: Determine whether a controlled anomaly is better explained by timezone conversion, clock skew, parser behavior, or source inconsistency.
steps: Compare at least two independent sources.
Write competing hypotheses and supporting/contradicting evidence.
practicals.solution: The correct result may be unresolved. The exercise evaluates the quality of evidence reasoning, not forced attribution.
practicals.output: Deliver a hypothesis table with evidence, contradiction, and confidence.

quiz.question: What does an anomalous timestamp prove?
options: Nothing by itself; it is an indicator for investigation
quiz.answer: Nothing by itself; it is an indicator for investigation
quiz.explanation: Multiple explanations can produce the same anomaly.

summary: Anomaly analysis requires corroboration.
Preserve originals and test competing explanations.

lessons.title: Derived Enrichment and Plaso Analysis Plugins
lessons.description: Use analysis plugins and tags as derived analytical aids.

notes.text: Plaso analysis plugins can enrich events with derived information. Its documentation includes sessionization and external hash/intelligence enrichment examples. Derived tags are useful for triage but should remain distinct from source records.

log2timeline.py --storage-file timeline.plaso image.raw
psort.py --analysis sessionize -o null timeline.plaso
psort.py -o dynamic --fields datetime,timestamp_desc,source,source_long,message,parser,tag -w timeline.csv timeline.plaso
External enrichment may have privacy, legal, and network-access implications. Use it only with appropriate authorization.

practicals.title: Sessionize a lab timeline
practicals.description: Apply Plaso's documented sessionize analysis plugin to a permitted lab timeline.
steps: Create or use a Plaso storage file.
practicals.solution:
log2timeline.py --storage-file timeline.plaso image.raw
psort.py --analysis sessionize -o null timeline.plaso
psort.py -o dynamic --fields datetime,timestamp_desc,source,source_long,message,parser,tag -w timeline.csv timeline.plaso
practicals.output: The exported timeline contains derived session tags. Exact grouping depends on the dataset and plugin behavior.

quiz.question: What is a Plaso analysis tag?
quiz.answer: Derived analytical information
quiz.explanation: Analysis plugins add derived context to events.

summary: Enrichment helps triage but does not replace source evidence.
External lookups must respect evidence-handling policy.

tasks.title: Investigate a Multi-Source Timeline Anomaly
tasks.description: Analyze filesystem, event-log, and network timestamps that disagree and determine which explanation is best supported.
tasks.problemStatement: Compare original and normalized values, test candidate explanations, and write a source-linked conclusion.
tasks.hint: Preserve every original timestamp before deriving corrected values.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The utility normalizes each source independently. The analyst then tests competing explanations instead of blindly correcting one source.

modules.title: Final Real-World Project: Forensic Timeline Correlation Workbench
modules.description: Final integrated practical assessment; no separate module tasks.

project.name: Forensic Timeline Correlation Workbench
project.description: Build a small, auditable Python CLI for authorized forensic lab datasets. It validates a normalized timeline CSV, parses offset-aware timestamps, reports data-quality errors, summarizes hourly activity density, performs bounded correlation around an analyst-selected anchor, and emits a JSON report containing an input hash and analytical metadata.
steps: Prepare a timeline CSV with timestamp, source, event_type, and message fields; preserve original source identifiers in additional columns.
Validate the input schema and reject timestamps without an explicit UTC offset.
Run the workbench and inspect parse errors before interpreting results.
Review the time range and hourly density to select candidate windows.
Use --target and --window-minutes to inspect events around a specific evidence-backed anchor.
Compare correlated events by source and event type; do not infer causality from proximity alone.
Retain the generated JSON report and its input SHA-256 as derived analytical artifacts.
Write a final finding that cites underlying source records and states clock, logging, parser, or collection limitations.

code.README.md:
# Forensic Timeline Correlation Workbench

Authorized-lab timeline analysis utility. Requires Python 3.11+ and only the standard library.
code.sample_timeline.csv:
timestamp,source,event_type,message
2026-01-15T10:00:00Z,windows-security,logon,Interactive logon observed
2026-01-15T10:02:00Z,filesystem,mtime,Report.docx modified
2026-01-15T10:03:30Z,browser,history,Visited https://example.invalid/report
2026-01-15T10:04:00Z,network,dns,Query for example.invalid
2026-01-15T10:10:00Z,windows-system,service,Service state changed

project.explanation: The loader requires timezone-aware timestamps, preserves the original string, and normalizes each event to UTC. The density function identifies activity windows without declaring them malicious. The correlation function returns observations inside an explicitly stated window around a chosen anchor. The report includes the input SHA-256, parse errors, event count, time range, density, and optional correlation results. It intentionally does not infer causality, identify a human actor, or silently correct clock skew. Those conclusions require source-specific forensic reasoning.
